Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 4:

"Record against those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah with disbelief." The intended meaning is disputation in falsehood, through reviling them and aiming to refute the truth and extinguish the light of Allah. This is indicated by ﴿And they dispute with falsehood, that they may thereby refute the truth﴾. As for disputing about them in order to clarify their obscure points and resolve their difficulties, and for scholars to contend over deriving their meanings and to refute the people of deviation by means of them and concerning them, that is the greatest struggle in the way of Allah. And his saying ﷺ: "Indeed, disputing about the Qur'an is disbelief" [[Narrated by al-Tayalisi. Through his chain, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, in the nineteenth section, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the wording "Do not dispute about the Qur'an, for disputing about it is disbelief." And on this theme there is a report from Abu Hurayra with the wording "Disputing about it is disbelief," in the Sahih and the Sunan.]] and his presenting it as a denunciation, even though he did not say "indeed disputing," is a distinction he makes between one kind of disputing and another. If you say: From where is the connection of his saying ﴿So let not their turning about in the land deceive you﴾ to what precedes it? I say: In that since they were witnessed against by Allah as disbelievers, and there is no one more wretched than the disbeliever in the sight of Allah, it is obligatory upon whoever recognizes this not to regard their condition as good in his eyes, nor to let their prosperity in their worldly life and their moving about in the lands with profitable trade and lucrative gains deceive him. Quraysh were like this, moving about in the lands of Syria and Yemen, possessing wealth with which they traded and profited, but the outcome of that is its end to perish, and behind it is the wretchedness of eternity. Then He set forth, as a parable for their denial, their enmity towards the messengers, their disputing in falsehood, and the evil end reserved for them, the example of the like of those nations, and of the punishment with which He seized them and the vengeance of His that He brought down upon their courtyard. And it has been recited: ﴿So let not [it] deceive you﴾.

The Confederates (al-Ahzab) are those who banded together against the messengers and opposed them, namely ʿAd, Thamud, Pharaoh, and others. Every nation of these peoples, from the people of Noah onward and the confederates, "plotted against their messenger" (wa-hammat kullu ummatin bi-rasulihim). It is also read as "bi-rasulihaa" (against its messenger).

"To seize him" (li-yakhudhuhu): so that they might gain power over him, and bring about his destruction and harm him with what they intended, whether torture or killing. A captive is called akhidh (seized). "And I seized them" (fa-akhadhtuhum): meaning that they intended to seize him, so the requital for their intention to seize him was that I seized them. "So how was My punishment?" (fa-kayfa kana ʿiqab): for you pass by their lands and their dwellings and witness the traces of that. This is a statement that carries the meaning of wonder (al-taʿjib).

That they are the companions of the Fire is in the position of a substitute (badal) for "the word of your Lord": that is, "Such was the decree that was made binding upon the disbelievers, that they are among the companions of the Fire." Its meaning: just as it was made binding that they be destroyed in this world by a punishment that uproots them, so it was made binding that they be destroyed by the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. Or it is in the accusative position, with the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) removed and the verb made to reach its object, meaning "because they are the companions of the Fire."

"Those who disbelieved" refers to Quraysh, and the meaning is: just as the destruction of those earlier nations was made binding, so the destruction of these was made binding, because one single cause unites them, namely that they are among the companions of the Fire.

It is recited as "kalimat" (plural: "words").

It is related that the bearers of the Throne have their feet in the lowest earth while their heads have pierced the Throne, and they are humbled, not raising their gaze.

It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not reflect upon the greatness of your Lord, but reflect upon what Allah has created of the angels." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi. Shahr ibn Hawshab reported that Ibn 'Abbas raised it, as a suspended (mu'allaq) report, and it is in Kitab al-'Azamah by Abu al-Fath.]] For there is a kind of angel called Israfil: one corner of the Throne is on his shoulder, his feet are in the lowest earth, and his head has passed through the seven heavens. Because of the greatness of Allah, he shrinks until he becomes like the wada'. [[His words "like the wada'": a bird smaller than the sparrow. (Ε)]] In a hadith: Allah, Exalted, commanded all the angels to go forth and return greeting the bearers of the Throne, honouring them above the rest of the angels. [[I have not found it.]] It was also said: Allah created the Throne from a green jewel, and between its two legs is the flapping of a swift bird's wing for eighty thousand years. It was said also: around the Throne are seventy thousand kinds of angels, who circle it glorifying (tahlil) and magnifying (takbir) Allah; behind them are seventy thousand rows standing, who have placed their hands upon their shoulders, raising their voices with tahlil and takbir; and behind them are a hundred thousand rows who have placed their right hands upon their left, and not one of them is except that he glorifies Allah with what the other does not glorify Him with. Ibn 'Abbas recited "al-'arsh" with a ḍamma on the 'ayn.

If you say: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and they believe in Him﴾, when it is not hidden from anyone that the bearers of the Throne and those around it of the angels, who glorify the praise of their Lord, are believers? [[Mahmud said: "If you say: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and they believe in Him﴾, when it is not hidden from anyone that the bearers of the Throne and those around it of the angels are believers in Allah, Exalted ... etc." Ahmad said: His statement is good, except that his argument from His words ﴿and they believe in Him﴾ that they are not witnesses (i.e., do not see Allah) does not prove that, because faith (iman) is assent (tasdiq), which does not require the absence of the one assented to. The proof is that it is valid to say one believes in signs even though they are witnessed, such as the splitting of the moon and the turning of the staff into a serpent. Al-Zamakhshari only strained this far in this forced reasoning because of a sickness in his heart, but he strayed far from the point. He asserted that the bearers of the Throne are not witnesses, by the proof of His words ﴿and they believe﴾, because the meaning of faith for him is assent to the unseen. Then from their not being witnesses he derives that the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, if seeing Him were valid, they would see Him; since they did not see Him, it follows that seeing Him is something reason does not validate. Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, commentary on Surah 40, verses 10–12:

They will be called out on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to them: ﴿The hatred of Allah toward you is greater﴾. The full sense is: "The hatred of Allah toward your souls is greater than your hatred of your own souls." The second mention is dropped because the first one is sufficient. ﴿When you were called﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by the first "hatred." The meaning is that it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: "Allah used to hate your souls, which commanded evil and disbelief, when the prophets called you to faith. You refused to accept it and chose disbelief over it, and that hatred is greater than the hatred you now feel for them while you are in the Fire, because you were brought into it by following their desires."

It is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri) that when they saw their evil deeds, they hated themselves, so they were told: "The hatred of Allah is greater." It was also said that the meaning is: "The hatred of Allah toward you now is greater than the hatred some of you have for others," like His saying ﴿Some of you will disbelieve in others and curse others﴾. ﴿When you were called﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil). *Al-maqt* (hatred) means intense aversion, and it is used here to express the strongest and most emphatic disapproval.

﴿You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice﴾. Some say it means two deaths and two lives, and others say two deaths and two lives in another sense.

By the two deaths he means: their being created dead at first, and their dying when their appointed terms end. By the two lives he means the first life and the life of resurrection. As a commentary on this, consider His saying: ﴿You were dead and He gave you life. Then He will cause you to die, then give you life again﴾. This is also what Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported.

If you ask: How is it correct to call their creation "causing them to die"? I answer: It is correct in the same way as when you say: "Glory be to Him who made the body of the gnat small and the body of the elephant large," or as when you say to the digger: "Narrow the mouth of the well and widen its bottom." There is no transition from large to small, nor from small to large, nor from narrow to wide, nor from wide to narrow. You simply intend the bringing into being with those qualities. The reason it is correct is that smallness and largeness are both possible for one created thing, with neither preferred over the other, and likewise narrowness and width. When the Creator chooses one of two possibilities while being able to choose either, He has made the created thing turn away from the other possibility, and turning away from it is like moving away from it.

[[Mahmud said: "One of the two deaths is their creation as dead beings at first, and the other is their dying when their appointed terms end." Then he said: "If you ask how He called their creation 'causing them to die,' he answers that it is like saying: 'Glory be to Him who made the body of the gnat small and the body of the elephant large,' and like saying to the digger: 'Narrow the mouth of the well and widen its bottom.' There is no transition from small to large or the reverse, nor from narrow to wide or the reverse. You simply intend the bringing into being with those qualities. The reason it is correct is that largeness and smallness are both possible for one created thing, and likewise narrowness and width. When the Creator chooses one of two possibilities while being able to choose the other, the choice is a turning away from the other while He was able to choose it."

Ahmad said: How well his words hold up here, since they agree with the reasoning of Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) in the question of a man who sells someone one of two specified weights, with the buyer obligated to one of them but the choice of which one left to him. Malik forbade this. Because the buyer was able to specify either one equally, when he specifies one of them by choice, his turning away from the other is treated as if he had chosen it first and then moved from it to this one. So if the sale ends with one being exchanged for the other when their equality is not known, this is the case our companions summarized as: whoever is given a choice between two things and chooses one of them is considered to have moved from one to the other. This principle has been mentioned before for a different purpose.]] equally. Then he has turned the created thing away from the other possibility, so his turning it away is like moving it from that possibility. Whoever takes the two deaths to be the one after the life of this world and the one after the life of the grave must affirm three lives, which contradicts the Qur'an, unless he stretches the text and treats one of them as not counted. Or he may claim that Allah gives them life in their graves, and that this life continues for them so that they never die afterward. Such a person would count them among those excepted from the Blast in His saying: ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾.

If you ask: How does this connect to His saying: ﴿So we have acknowledged our sins﴾? I answer: They denied the resurrection and so disbelieved, and countless sins followed from that, because whoever does not fear the consequence gives free rein to sins. Its meaning: a herald will call out and say, "Whose is the dominion today?" and the people of the gathering will answer him, "To God, the One, the Subduer." It has been said: God will gather the creatures on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, a white land like a silver ingot, in which He was never disobeyed, "and the first thing spoken will be that a herald calls out: 'Whose is the dominion today? To God, the One, the Subduer. Today every soul will be recompensed...'" (40:17), the verse. This indicates that the caller is the one who answers.

He shows you His signs: from the wind, the clouds, the thunder, the lightning, the thunderbolts and the like. "Provision" (al-rizq) means rain, because it is its cause. "None takes heed except one who turns back (in repentance)": none is admonished or takes a lesson from the signs of God except one who repents of polytheism and returns to God, for the stubborn one has no way to remembrance or admonition. Then He said, addressing those who turn back: "So call upon God," that is, worship Him, "making the religion sincerely His," free of polytheism, "even though the unbelievers among your enemies, those who are not upon your religion, are enraged by it."

"Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne, He casts the Spirit": these are three predicates, according to His saying "He" (huwa), arranged after His saying "who shows you," or they are predicates of an omitted subject (mubtada'); they differ in definiteness and indefiniteness. It was also read as "Exalted in degrees" in the accusative, as a expression of praise (nasb 'ala al-madh).

"Exalted in degrees" is like His saying, "Possessor of the ascending stairways" (dhi al-ma'arij), and they are the ascents of the angels until they reach the Throne, and this is evidence of His might and sovereignty. It is related from Ibn Jubayr: "a heaven above a heaven, and the Throne above them all." It is also permissible that it be an expression of the exaltedness of His station and the loftiness of His authority, just as "Lord of the Throne" is an expression of His dominion. It has been said: they are the degrees of His reward which He bestows upon His friends in Paradise.

"The Spirit from His command": the one that is the cause of life, from His command, meaning the revelation, which is a command to good and an impulse toward it, so He metaphorically named it a spirit, just as He said, "Is one who was dead and We gave him life...?" (6:122), "that he may warn of the Meeting" (liyunthira). Or the one upon whom it is cast is the Messenger, or the Spirit. It was read "that you may warn" (litunthira), meaning: that the Spirit may warn, since it is feminine, or addressing the Messenger. It was also read "that He may warn" (liyunthira) in the passive voice, "of the Day of Meeting" (yawm al-talaq), which is the Day of Resurrection, because the creatures meet on it. It has been said: the people of heaven and the people of earth meet on it. It has been said: the worshipped and the worshipper.

"The Day they will come forth" (yawm hum bariziin): manifest, nothing concealing them, whether mountain, hill or building, because the earth will be leveled, a bare plain; nor will they have garments upon them, but they will be naked and exposed, as came in the hadith: "They will be gathered naked, barefoot and uncircumcised" [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her.]]. "Nothing of them is hidden from God": of their deeds and conditions. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him: "Nothing of them is hidden from Him."

If you say: His saying "Nothing of them is hidden from God" is an explanation and confirmation of their being exposed, and God is not hidden from anything of them whether they are exposed or not, so what is its meaning? I say: its meaning is that in the world they used to imagine, when they concealed themselves behind walls and screens, that God did not see them and that their deeds were hidden from Him; so today they pass from exposure and disclosure to a state in which they will not imagine what they used to imagine. God the Exalted said: "But you thought that God does not know much of what you do" (41:22). And He said: "They conceal themselves from people, but they do not conceal themselves from God" (4:108). That is because they knew that people could see them, and they thought that God could not see them; and this is the meaning of His saying, "And they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer." "Whose is the dominion today? To God, the One, the Subduer" is a report of what will be asked on that day and of what is answered. Its meaning: a herald will call out and say, "Whose is the dominion today?" and the people of the gathering will answer him, "To God, the One, the Subduer." It has been said: God will gather the creatures on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, a white land like a silver ingot, in which He was never disobeyed, "and the first thing spoken will be that a herald calls out: 'Whose is the dominion today? To God, the One, the Subduer. Today every soul will be recompensed...'" (40:17), the verse. This indicates that the caller is the one who answers.

When he established that sovereignty belongs to God alone on that Day, he enumerated the consequences of that: that every soul is recompensed for what it earned; that injustice is secure from occurring, because God is not unjust to His servants; and that the reckoning will not be delayed, because God is not preoccupied by one account from another, so He reckons all creation at one time, and He is the swiftest of reckoners. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: when He takes up their reckoning, the people of Paradise will not take a midday rest (qaylula) except in it, nor the people of the Fire except in it. [[His words "the people of Paradise will not take a midday rest except in it": whoever said "yaqīl qaylūla" (takes a midday rest). (ʿ)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 18:

Al-Āzifah (the Imminent Day): the Resurrection. It is so called because of its approaching (azūf), meaning its nearness. It is also permissible that by "the Day of the Imminent" is meant the time of the imminent calamity (al-khaṭṭah al-āzifah), which is their approach to entering the Fire. At that moment their hearts rise from their places and cling to their throats (ḥanājir), so they neither leave, so that they die, nor return to their places, so that they breathe and find relief. Rather, they are stuck like a choking lump (kash-shajā), as the Most High said: ﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be darkened.﴾ [Q 67:27]

If you ask: with what is kāẓimīn (choking with grief) in the accusative?

I say: it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the people (aṣḥāb al-qulūb) in meaning, because the meaning is: "when their hearts are at their throats, choking upon them." It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause referring to the hearts, meaning that the hearts are choking with distress and anguish within them while reaching the throats. The plural of kāẓim is in the sound masculine plural form (jam' al-salāmah) because it has been described with kaẓm (choking), which is an action of rational beings, as the Most High said: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Q 12:4] and He said: ﴿their necks remained humbled before it﴾ [Q 26:4]. The reading of the one who reads kāẓimūn supports this. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause referring to His saying "and warn them," meaning: "and warn them while they are about to choke," like His saying: ﴿Enter it to abide therein﴾ [Q 39:72].

Al-ḥamīm: the loving and compassionate friend. Al-muṭā‘: a metaphorical usage for the intercessor (al-mushaffa‘), because the true nature of obedience is like the true nature of command, in that it is only due to one who is above you.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Q 40:18]?

I say: it may be that the negation encompasses both intercession and obedience together, and it may be that it encompasses obedience without intercession. [[Mahmūd said: "It may be that what is negated is the intercessor, who is the described one, together with his attribute, which is obedience; and it may be that what is negated is the attribute, which is obedience, while the intercessor is established." Aḥmad said: the possibility arises only from the fact that the negation has entered upon the combined unit of the described and the attribute. Negating a whole can be achieved by negating each of its two parts, and likewise by negating one of them. However, the intended meaning here, as he said, is the negation of both matters together. He said: the benefit of mentioning the described is that it serves as evidence for the negation of the attribute, because when the described is negated, the attribute is certainly negated. I say: so it is as if he negated the attribute twice from two different aspects.]] Just as you say: "I have no book for sale" (mā ‘indī kitābun yubā‘): this may negate only the sale, meaning that you have a book but do not sell it, or it may negate both together, meaning that you have no book and it is not for sale. Similar to it is the verse:

"And you do not see the lizard (ḍabb) entering its hole there" (wa-lā tarā al-ḍabba bihā yanjaḥirr).

It intends: negating the lizard and its entering its hole.

If you ask: on which of the two possibilities must it be understood?

I say: it must be understood as negating both matters together, because the intercessors are the friends of God, and the friends of God do not love or approve except those whom God loves and approves, and God does not love the wrongdoers. Thus they do not love them, and when they do not love them they do not support them nor intercede for them.

The Most High said: ﴿And for the wrongdoers there will be no helpers﴾ [Q 2:270], and He said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [Q 21:28]. Also, intercession is only for an increase in grace (al-tafaḍḍul). [[His saying "intercession is only for an increase in grace" is the view of the Mu‘tazilah. As for the People of the Sunnah, it is also for leaving the Fire, as established in the discussion of tawḥīd. The hadith of intercession is well known. Yes, the disbelievers have no exit from the Fire. (ʿ)]] The people of grace and its increase are only the people of reward, as evidenced by the Most High's saying: ﴿and He will increase them from His bounty﴾ [Q 42:26]. It is related from al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "By Allah, they will have no intercessor at all."

If you ask: the purpose is achieved by mentioning the intercessor and negating him, so what is the benefit of mentioning this attribute and negating it?

I say: mentioning it has a great benefit, which is that it has been joined to it, so that the negation of the described stands in the place of evidence for the negation of the attribute, because the attribute cannot be realized without its described. This removes the suspicion of the existence of the described. Its explanation: when you are rebuked for staying back from the raid and you say: "I have no horse to ride, nor do I have a weapon with which to fight," you have made the absence of a horse and the lack of a weapon a preventing cause for riding and fighting, as if you were saying: "How can riding and fighting be possible for me when I have no horse and no weapon?" Likewise His saying ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ means: how can intercession be realized when there is no intercessor? So the mention of intercession, and the evidence for its impossibility by the absence of an intercessor, was placed as a substitute for the negation of the intercessor in the place of the well-known matter [[His saying "in the place of the well-known matter" means that which the listener knows and accepts, as is the case with evidence for a claim. When the absence of an intercessor is well known, it cannot be supposed that it is otherwise, and on this basis his earlier statement becomes clear: this removes the suspicion of the existence of the described. (ʿ)]], not a disputed matter whose opposite should not be supposed.

Al-Khā'inah: an attribute of the glance (naẓrah), or a verbal noun meaning treachery (khiyānah), like al-'āfiyah meaning al-mu'āfāh. The intended meaning is the furtive glance at what is not lawful, as the people of suspicion do. It is not good to take al-khā'inah as referring to the eyes, because His words ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ do not agree with that. [Maḥmūd said: "al-khā'inah is either an attribute of the glance or a verbal noun like al-'āfiyah." He said: "It is not good to take al-khā'inah as referring to the eyes," because the words of the Exalted ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾ do not agree with it. Aḥmad said: It does not agree with it because, on this reading, the meaning of "treacherous eyes" would be the eyes that are treacherous, whereas what is set against the eyes is the breasts, not what the breasts conceal. By contrast, in the first interpretation, what is meant is the glances of the eyes, which matches the hidden things of the breasts.] If you ask: with what is His saying ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ connected?

I say: it is a report among the reports that begin with His saying ﴿He is the One who shows you﴾, like ﴿He casts the Spirit﴾. But ﴿He casts the Spirit﴾ was given a reason by His saying ﴿so that he may warn of the Day of Mutual Meeting﴾, and then the discussion digressed to describe the conditions of the Day of Meeting, down to His saying ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾. So it is distant, because of that, from its counterparts.

And Allah judges with truth. That is: the One who has these attributes and states does not judge except with truth and justice,

because He is free of any need for injustice. As for your gods, they judge nothing. This is mockery of them, for that which is not described as having power is not said of it, "it judges" or "it does not judge."

Indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing: this confirms His words "He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal," and it is a warning to them that He hears what they say and sees what they do, and that He will punish them for it. It is also an allusion to what they call upon besides Allah, that they neither hear nor see. It is also read "yadʿūna" (they call upon) and "tadʿūna" (you call upon), with the ya and the ta.

**[Verse 21: "...they were stronger than them..."]** The pronoun *fasl* (separating pronoun, *damir al-fasl*) is used here: *hum* between *kanu* and *ashadda*, as in *kanu hum ashadda minhum*.

If you object that the separating pronoun should only come between two definite terms, but here it comes between a definite term and an indefinite one (*ashadd minhum*), the answer is that *ashadd* resembles a definite noun in that the definite article *al-* cannot be attached to it. It is therefore treated as if it were definite.

It is recited as *minkum* (from you), and that is how it is written in the codices of the people of Shaam (Syria).

*Wa-athāran* (and traces/monuments) means their fortresses, their palaces, their numbers, and whatever is described as strong among their remains.

Or they meant: "more numerous in traces," as in the verse:

*Wa-ra'ayta zawjaka fi al-wughā... mutaqallidan sayfan wa-rumḥan*
"I saw your husband in the battle, girded with a sword and a spear."

*Al-wughā* means war. *Rumḥan* is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by the context, meaning: "girded with a sword, and carrying a spear."

It is also related with a different first half-line:

*Yā layta zawjaka qad ghadā*
"Would that your husband had gone off..." That is, he went to war in the morning, wearing his weapons.

﴿Leave me, that I may kill Moses.﴾ Whenever he (Pharaoh) intended to kill him, they (his people) restrained him by saying: "He is not one to be feared. He is weaker and lesser than that. He is only one of the sorcerers, and only a sorcerer like himself can stand against such a man." They would also say: "If you kill him, you will create doubt among the people, who will believe that you were unable to oppose him with argument." Apparently, Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, was certain that he (Moses) was a prophet and that what he brought were signs, not sorcery. But the man had cunning and shrewdness, and he was a bloodthirsty killer who shed blood over trivial matters. So how could he not kill someone whom he sensed would tear up his throne and destroy his kingdom? But he feared that if he intended to kill him, he would be hastened to destruction. Killing him would cause people to suspect that you killed him out of fear.' He wished to conceal his fear of killing him by saying to them: 'Leave me to kill him,' so that they would restrain him, and the restraint from killing would be attributed to them, not to his anxiety and fear. His words ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾ indicate his fear of him, and this is among his well-known deceptions." Ahmad said: "This is of the same kind as his words ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band, and indeed they have enraged us, and indeed we are all wary﴾. They worshipped him and worshipped idols, as evidenced by His words ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾. ﴿And corruption on the earth﴾: factionalism and mutual chaos which take away security and bring ruin to the farms, livelihoods, and means of living, and destroy people through killing and loss. It is also read "yuzhira" (that he may make appear), from "adhhara" (to cause to appear), and "al-fasad" (the corruption) is then in the accusative, meaning: "Moses makes corruption appear." It is also read "yazhara" with doubled ẓā' and hā', from "tazahara," meaning "tataba'a wa ta'awana" (to follow in succession and to cooperate).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 27:

When Musa (peace be upon him) heard what Fir'awn (Pharaoh) had done regarding the talk of killing him, he said to his people: ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge in Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾ His saying "and your Lord" contains an incitement for them to follow his example, so that they seek refuge in Allah with the same refuge he sought, and hold fast to reliance upon Him with the same holding fast. He said ﴿from every arrogant one﴾ so that his seeking refuge would include Fir'awn and others among the tyrants, and so that it would be in the manner of allusion, which is more eloquent. By "arrogance" he meant refusal to submit to the truth, which is the worst kind of arrogance and the clearest evidence of its possessor's baseness and the abasement of his soul, and of his extreme injustice and oppression. He said ﴿who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾ because when a man combines arrogance, denial of recompense, and lack of concern for the outcome, he has gathered the causes of hardness of heart and boldness against Allah and His servants, and leaves no great sin uncommitted. 

"ʿadhtu" (I sought refuge) and "laadhtu" (I clung/took refuge) are synonyms (akhawan). It is also recited as ʿat, with idgham (assimilation of the two letters).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 40, verse 28:**

A man who believes. It is also read as *rajul* with the *jim* pronounced with a sukun, as in *'adud* for *'add* (arm). He was a Copt and a cousin of Pharaoh. He believed in Moses secretly.

It is also said that he was an Israelite. The phrase ﴿from among the family of Pharaoh﴾ describes "a man," or it is connected to *yaktumu* ("he conceals"), meaning: he conceals his faith from the family of Pharaoh. His name was Sam'an or Habib. It is also said that it was Kharbil or Hizqil.

The apparent view is that he was from the family of Pharaoh, because the believers among the Children of Israel did not speak out or make it known. The evidence for this is Pharaoh's saying: ﴿I will kill their sons who believe with him﴾ (Qur'an 40:25). And the believer's saying ﴿Who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ (Qur'an 40:29) is clear evidence that he was giving sincere counsel to his people. The phrase ﴿that he says﴾ means "because he says."

This is a great rebuke and a severe reproach, as if he said: Do you commit the abominable act of killing a soul which Allah has forbidden, while you have no reason at all for committing it except the word of truth which he has uttered, namely his saying ﴿My Lord is Allah﴾ (Qur'an 40:28)? Yet he did not come with a single proof to confirm his claim, but with many clear proofs from the One to whom lordship is attributed, and He is your Lord, not only his. This is a way of drawing them toward acknowledging Him, to soften their obstinacy and break their pride.

[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The apparent view is that the man was from the family of Pharaoh; it is also said that he was from the Children of Israel. The phrase *min Al Fir'awn* ("from the family of Pharaoh") is connected to *yaktumu*, its meaning being: he conceals his faith from the family of Pharaoh. This is far-fetched, because the faith of the Children of Israel was apparent and widespread. This believer indeed led them, step by step, into faith by bearing witness to the truth of Moses, peace be upon him, by bringing from the One to whom lordship is attributed many clear proofs, not just one proof. He expressed it in the definite form (*al-bayyinat*), meaning: the great proofs which you have witnessed and recognized as such, so as to soften their obstinacy and break their pride..." etc.]

Ahmad [ibn al-Munayyir] said: He has indeed understood well and perceived the secrets of this statement. The placing of the liar before the truthful here is paralleled by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And a witness from among her people testified: If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is of the truthful﴾ (Qur'an 12:26–27). Here the witness mentioned the sign of her truthfulness before the sign of Joseph's truthfulness, even though the truthful one was Joseph and not her, in order to remove suspicion and dispel doubt, and to assert confidently that the truth was with him. The delay does not harm him for this benefit.

Similar to this procedure of removing suspicion is what occurred in the story of Joseph with his brother, when he began with their containers before the container of his brother, until it is said that when he reached it he said: "O Allah, this one did not steal, nor is he of the nature of a thief." Their hearts were reassured and the suspicion was removed from Joseph, lest he had intended this. Then they said: "By Allah, we will search him," and he brought it out from his bag.

As for the phrase ﴿with clear proofs﴾, he means by "clear proofs" the great signs which you were accustomed to and which you witnessed. Then he took them to task by argument, in the manner of division (*taqsim*), saying: It is not free of being either a liar or truthful. ﴿If he is a liar, his lie will be upon him﴾, meaning his lie will return to him and its harm will not go beyond him. ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾, if you oppose him.

If you say: Why did he say ﴿some of what he promises you﴾, when he is a truthful prophet, and what he promises them must befall them entirely, not partly? I say: Because in arguing with the adversaries of Moses and in dealing with them, he needed to flatter them and to placate them (*yulawisuhum*), and to take the path of fairness in speech, and to approach them from the direction of sincere counsel. So he said what he knew was closer to their acceptance of his words and more inclined to their belief in him and their acceptance from him. He said: ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾. This is the speech of one who is fair in his statement, not one who exaggerates. He said this so that they would listen to him and not reject him. For when he assumed that he was truthful, he had already affirmed that he was truthful in everything he promised; but he followed it with ﴿some of what he promises you﴾ so as to diminish part of his right in the apparent wording, so that they would see that this is not the speech of one who gives him his full right, let alone one who is partisan toward him, or one who throws stones at him from behind. The placing of the liar before the truthful is also of this kind, and likewise the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar﴾ (Qur'an 40:28).

If you say: It is reported from Abu 'Ubaydah that he explained *al-ba'd* ("some") as *al-kull* ("all"), and he recited the verse of Labid:

*Tarrak amkinatin idha lam arddaha*
*aw yartabit ba'd al-nufus hamamuha*

I say: If the report from him is authentic, then what al-Mazini said about the issue of *al-'alqa* applies to it: "He was too dull to understand what I say to him." ﴿Indeed Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor﴾ may mean: he was a transgressing liar whom Allah abandoned and destroyed, and his affair did not succeed, so they would be rid of him. And if he were a transgressing liar, Allah would not have guided him to prophethood, nor supported him with clear proofs.

It is also said: What Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) endured from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was harder than this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulated the House, and when he finished they met him, took hold of the folds of his cloak and said to him: "You are the one who forbids us from what our fathers worshipped?" He said: "I am that one." Then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up, embraced him from behind, and said, raising his voice while his eyes streamed with tears: "Will you kill a man for saying 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord?" until they released him. [Al-Nasa'i narrated it through the chain of Hisham from Urwah from his father from 'Amr ibn al-'As. Ibn Hibban narrated it through the chain of Yahya ibn Urwah from Urwah from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, more complete than it. I say: al-Bukhari recorded something similar to them in suspended form.]

It is reported from Ja'far al-Sadiq that the believer of the family of Pharaoh said that secretly, whereas Abu Bakr said it openly.

ظاهِرِينَ فِي الْأَرْضِ: "dominant in the land," i.e., in the land of Egypt, exalted over the Children of Israel. The meaning is: you have the kingship of Egypt, and you have risen over the people and subjugated them. So do not ruin your affairs for yourselves, and do not expose yourselves to the might and punishment of God, for you have no power against Him if He comes upon you, and no one will protect you from Him.

And he said ﴿He will help us﴾ and ﴿has come to us﴾, because he was among them by kinship, and so that they would know that the counsel he gives them is something in which he has a share with them.

﴿I show you only what I see﴾: that is, I give you counsel only according to what I see, namely, killing him. I deem nothing right except killing him, and what you are saying is not correct.

﴿And I guide you only to the way of rectitude﴾: he means the way of correctness and righteousness.

Or, the meaning is: "I only inform you of what I know to be right, and I withhold nothing from it, and I do not conceal from you anything contrary to what I display," meaning that his tongue and heart agree on what he says, and he lied. He was in fact sensing a severe fear from Moses, but he was feigning boldness. Had he not sensed it, he would not have consulted anyone, nor would the matter have stopped at mere indication.

It is recited as ﴿al-rashād﴾, the pattern fa'āl from rashida (with kasra), like 'allām; or from rashada (with fatha), like 'abbād. It has been said that it is from arshada, like jabbār from ajbara, but this is not so, because fa'āl from af'ala has come only in a number of words, such as darrāk, sārr, qassār, and ḥabbār, and analogy is not valid on the basis of the rare. It is also permissible that it be a nisba to rushd, like 'awwāj and battāt, without regard to a verb.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verses 30–31:

﴿Like the day of the factions﴾: "like their days." Because he attached it to "the factions" and explained them as the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud, and it was not ambiguous that each faction had a day of destruction, he limited it to the singular of the plural, since the genitive construction made that unnecessary. As in his saying:

"Eat in some of your belly, so that you may refrain [from food]
For your time is a time of famine (khamīṣ)."

That is: "eat in some of your bellies." He used the singular "belly" to avoid ambiguity, meaning: do not fill them; if you obey me, you will abstain from food. ʿAffa yaʿiffu, with the vowel of the imperfect's ʿayn being kasra, from the pattern ḍaraba yaḍribu. Then he said: "for your time," meaning: I commanded you to that because your time is barren (mujdib).

Al-Khamīṣ: the one whose belly is lean. He likened the barren time to a hungry man by way of metonymy (kināya), and describing it with emaciation is an imaginative depiction (takhyīl) of that.

Al-Zajjaj said: "like the day of a faction, a faction." Their habit (daʾb): their diligence in their work, namely disbelief, denial and all other sins, and that this was constant and perpetual on their part, never ceasing. There must be an elided genitive (muḍāf maḥdhūf); he means: like the recompense of their habit. If you ask: with what is the second "mithl" in the accusative? I answer: it is in apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to the first "mithl," because the last thing the genitive construction covered is "the people of Noah." Had you said, "God destroyed the factions: the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud," it would only be an apposition to the genitive of "people" attached to proper names, and that ruling extends to the first element covered by the genitive construction.

﴿And God does not desire injustice for the servants﴾: meaning that their destruction was justice and equity, because they deserved it through their deeds. This is more emphatic than His saying ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾, in that He made the negated element the desire of injustice, because one who is far from desiring injustice is further still from committing it. And in that He made "injustice" indefinite, as if He negated that He desires any injustice whatsoever for His servants. [Note by the editor: his saying "as if He negated that He desires any injustice for His servants" is according to the Mu'tazila's view that God does not do evil nor desire it, and that desire (irāda) means approval (riḍā). According to Ahl al-Sunna, God creates evil and desires it as He does good, but does not approve of evil; approval is other than desire in their view, as established in the discussion of Tawhid. (ʿ)]. It is also permissible that its meaning is like the meaning of His saying ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, meaning: God does not desire for His servants that they wrong one another; that is, He destroyed them because they were wrongdoers. [Mahmud said: "It is permissible that its meaning is the meaning of: 'And your Lord is not unjust to the servants.' This is more emphatic, for when He does not desire injustice, He is further from committing it; and in making "injustice" indefinite too, it is as if He negated that He desires any injustice whatsoever for His servants. He said: It is also permissible that its meaning is like His saying ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, so the meaning is that God does not desire for His servants that they do wrong, because He blamed them for being wrongdoers." Ahmad said: this is of the first rank; but the school of Ahl al-Sunna regarding God's will has already been stated, in contrast to this view and its adherents.]

The Day of Mutual Calling (al-Tanad). This is what God Most High relates in Surah al-A'raf in His words: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire, and the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾. It is also permissible that their outcry be with ﴿woe﴾ and ﴿destruction﴾. It has been read with the intensive form (tashdid).

It means that some of them flee from others, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾. It is related from Qatadah: turning away from the place of reckoning toward the Fire. And it is related from Mujahid: fleeing from the Fire, not able to escape.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 34–35:

He is Yusuf ibn Ya'qub, peace be upon them both. It was also said: he is Yusuf ibn Ibrahim [[His statement "and it was said he is Yusuf ibn Ibrahim": the wording of al-Nasafi is Afrathim. (ʿA.)]] ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub.

He established a prophet among them for twenty years. It was also said that the Pharaoh of Musa is the Pharaoh of Yusuf, who lived on until his time.

It was also said: he is another Pharaoh. He rebuked them, saying: Yusuf came to you with the clear signs, and you doubted them, and you remained doubting and disbelieving until, when he died, you said: "Allah will never send after him a messenger" [Qur'an 40:34], a judgment from your own selves, without proof and without any prior resolve on your part to deny the messengers. So when a messenger came to you, you denied and rejected him, on the basis of your false judgment which you had established. Their saying "Allah will never send after him a messenger" is not an affirmation of the prophethood of Yusuf, for how could it be, when they had doubted it and disbelieved in it? Rather, it is a denial of a messenger after him, added to the denial of his own prophethood. It is also read: "Will Allah not send...", with the interrogative hamza placed before the negative particle, as if some of them were confirming to one another the negation of a sending. Then He said: "Thus Allah leaves astray" [Qur'an 40:34], i.e., like this manifest abandonment, Allah forsakes every transgressor in his disobedience who is in doubt about his religion, "those who dispute" [Qur'an 40:35] is a substitute for "one who is a transgressor" [Qur'an 40:34]. [[His statement "i.e., like this manifest abandonment": the Mu'tazilites interpret misguidance as forsaking and leaving, based on their doctrine that Allah does not create evil. The People of the Sunna interpret it as the creation of error in the heart, based on the premise that He, exalted is He, creates evil as He creates good, as explained in the section on Tawhid. (ʿA.)]] If you say: how is it permissible to substitute it for him, when the one is plural and that is singular? I say: because he does not mean one transgressor in particular; it is as if he said: every transgressor. If you say: then what is the subject of "it is greatly hateful" [Qur'an 40:35]? I say: the pronoun referring to "one who is a transgressor." If you say:

Did you not say that it is plural, which is why "those who dispute" was substituted for it? I say: Yes, it is plural in meaning, but in wording it is singular, so the substitution is taken according to its meaning, and the pronoun referring back to it according to its wording, and this is not unprecedented. [[Mahmud said: "'Those who dispute' is a substitute for 'one who is a transgressor,' because what is meant is every transgressor. Its substitution was permitted according to the meaning of 'man,' not its wording. He said: If you say, what is the subject of 'it is greatly hateful'? He answered that it is the pronoun referring to 'one who is a transgressor,' so the substitute is taken by meaning and the pronoun by wording, and this is not unprecedented." End of his words. Ahmad said: What he mentioned is treating the wording of "man" after treating its meaning, and this is among what I previously noted the grammarians find strange. It is better to avoid this in the i'rab of the Qur'an, for it involves obscurity after clarity, whereas the known practice in eloquent recitation is the reverse. The correct view is to make the pronoun in his statement "it is greatly hateful" refer back to the verbal noun of the preceding verb, namely his statement "they dispute," its estimate being: "their disputing is greatly hateful in wrath," and to make "those who" the subject with an implied omitted genitive, its estimate being: "the disputing of those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah," and the pronoun in his statement "it is greatly hateful in wrath" returns to the omitted disputing, and the clause is a subject and predicate. Similar to this, in omitting the verbal noun and building the speech upon it, is His statement, exalted is He: "Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like one who believed in Allah" [Qur'an 9:19], according to one of its interpretations, and there are many like it. Beyond that there are other aspects free of what leads to the previous aspect. So the preferable course is to avoid it, to take it by wording at times and by meaning at others, and there are parallels to this. It is also permissible to make "those who dispute" the subject, and there must in this case be an omitted genitive to which the pronoun in "greatly hateful" returns, its estimate being: "the disputing of those who dispute is greatly hateful in wrath," and it may be that "those who dispute" is the subject, and "without any authority that came to them" is the predicate, and the subject of "is hateful" is his statement "thus," i.e., the disputing is greatly hateful in wrath like that disputing; and "Allah seals" is a new, independent statement. Whoever says "their disputing is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah" has omitted the subject, and the subject cannot be omitted. In "greatly hateful in wrath" there is a kind of wonder and magnification of their disputing, and a testimony that its departure from the bounds of its ambiguity is among the major sins.

It is also read: "sultan" with a damma on the lam. It is also read: "qalb" with tanwin. The heart is described with arrogance and tyranny because it is the seat and source of them, as you say: "the eye saw" and "the ear heard." Similar to it is His statement, exalted is He: "Its heart is sinful" [Qur'an 2:283], though the sinner is the whole person. It is also permissible that there is an omitted genitive: i.e., over every heart that is arrogant, making the attribute belong to the possessor of the heart.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verses 36–37:

It has been said: al-sarh (the lofty structure) is a visible building that is not hidden from the observer, however far away he may be. They derived it from sarah al-shay'(the thing became manifest) when a thing becomes apparent. And asbab al-samawat (the means to the heavens) are their paths, their gates, and whatever leads to them. Everything that brings you to something is a sabab (means) to it, like a rope and the like. If you ask: what is the benefit of this repetition? Would it not have sufficed to say: "so that I may reach the means of the heavens"? I answer: when a thing is first stated in general terms and then made clear, this magnifies its importance. So when he wished to magnify what he hoped to reach of the means to the heavens, he stated it in general terms and then clarified it. Moreover, since reaching them was a wondrous matter, he wished to present it to a soul eager for it, so that the listener would give it its due of amazement. So he made it vague in order to stir the soul of Haman toward it, and then he clarified it. It is also read fa-attali'a with the accusative (naṣb), as a response to the optative (tarajji), likening tarajji to tamanni (wishing). A similar case is the adornment and the turning away: ﴿Zuyyina li-Fir'awna su'u 'amalihi wa-ṣuddda 'ani al-sabil﴾ (Fir'awn's evil deed was made attractive to him, and he was turned away from the way). The one who adorned it may be Satan through his whispering, as in His saying, ﴿wa-zayyana lahumu al-shaytanu a'malahum fa-sadahum 'ani al-sabil﴾ (Satan made their deeds attractive to them and turned them from the way), or it may be Allah, the Exalted, by way of causation, since He empowered Satan and gave him respite. Similarly, ﴿zayyanna lahum a'malahum fa-hum ya'mahun﴾ (We made their deeds attractive to them, so they wander blindly). It is also read: wa-zuyyina lahu su'u 'amalihi (and the evil of his deed was made attractive to him), with the verb in the active voice and the subject being Allah, the Exalted, indicated by His saying, ﴿ila ilahi Musa﴾ (to the god of Musa). And ṣudda, with fatḥ, ḍamm, or kasr on the ṣād, is due to the transfer of the vowel of the ʿayn to the fāʾ, as in qīla (it was said). Al-tabab means loss and destruction.

Ṣadd is a verbal noun (maṣdar) coordinated with (ma'ṭūf 'alā) su'u 'amalihi. "And he and his people turned away."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verses 36–37:

It has been said: al-sarh (the lofty structure) is a visible building that is not hidden from the observer, however far away he may be. They derived it from sarah al-shay'(the thing became manifest) when a thing becomes apparent. And asbab al-samawat (the means to the heavens) are their paths, their gates, and whatever leads to them. Everything that brings you to something is a sabab (means) to it, like a rope and the like. If you ask: what is the benefit of this repetition? Would it not have sufficed to say: "so that I may reach the means of the heavens"? I answer: when a thing is first stated in general terms and then made clear, this magnifies its importance. So when he wished to magnify what he hoped to reach of the means to the heavens, he stated it in general terms and then clarified it. Moreover, since reaching them was a wondrous matter, he wished to present it to a soul eager for it, so that the listener would give it its due of amazement. So he made it vague in order to stir the soul of Haman toward it, and then he clarified it. It is also read fa-attali'a with the accusative (naṣb), as a response to the optative (tarajji), likening tarajji to tamanni (wishing). A similar case is the adornment and the turning away: ﴿Zuyyina li-Fir'awna su'u 'amalihi wa-ṣuddda 'ani al-sabil﴾ (Fir'awn's evil deed was made attractive to him, and he was turned away from the way). The one who adorned it may be Satan through his whispering, as in His saying, ﴿wa-zayyana lahumu al-shaytanu a'malahum fa-sadahum 'ani al-sabil﴾ (Satan made their deeds attractive to them and turned them from the way), or it may be Allah, the Exalted, by way of causation, since He empowered Satan and gave him respite. Similarly, ﴿zayyanna lahum a'malahum fa-hum ya'mahun﴾ (We made their deeds attractive to them, so they wander blindly). It is also read: wa-zuyyina lahu su'u 'amalihi (and the evil of his deed was made attractive to him), with the verb in the active voice and the subject being Allah, the Exalted, indicated by His saying, ﴿ila ilahi Musa﴾ (to the god of Musa). And ṣudda, with fatḥ, ḍamm, or kasr on the ṣād, is due to the transfer of the vowel of the ʿayn to the fāʾ, as in qīla (it was said). Al-tabab means loss and destruction.

Ṣadd is a verbal noun (maṣdar) coordinated with (ma'ṭūf 'alā) su'u 'amalihi. "And he and his people turned away."

Said: "Follow me, and I will guide you to the path of right conduct." He first stated it in general terms, then explained it. He began with a condemnation of this worldly life and a diminishing of its worth, because inclining toward it (al-ikhlad ilayha) is the root of all evil, and from it branches out everything that leads to the displeasure of God and brings wretchedness in the end. He followed this with an exaltation of the Hereafter and an informing of them of its reality, that it is the true homeland and the lasting abode, and he mentioned the deeds, both the evil and the good, and the outcome of each. This was so that he would deter them from what destroys and spur them toward what brings them near (to God). Then he weighed the two calls against each other: a call to the religion of God, whose fruit is salvation, and their call to taking rivals (to God), whose end is the Fire. He gave warning, admonished, and exerted himself in this and gathered (his efforts). Undoubtedly, God singled him out from the family of Pharaoh and made him a proof against them and a lesson for those who take heed, and this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and there befell the people of Pharaoh an evil torment.﴾ In this there is also clear evidence that the man was of the family of Pharaoh. Al-rashad is the opposite of al-ghayy (error). And in it is an allusion, close to explicit statement, that what Pharaoh and his people were upon is the path of error.

Translation:

"He is not recompensed except with its like, for an increase over the measure of the recompense for an evil deed is ugly, since it is injustice. As for an increase over the measure of the recompense for a good deed, it is good, since it is bounty. It is read: 'They will enter' and 'They will enter [Paradise] without reckoning' (bi-ghayri ḥisāb), which is set in opposition to 'except with its like.' That is to say: the recompense for an evil deed has a reckoning and a measure, lest it exceed what is deserved; but the recompense for a righteous deed is without measure and without reckoning, rather whatever increase you wish beyond what is due, in abundance and in breadth."

**Question:** Why did he repeat the call to his people? And why was the conjunction *wa* (and) used with the third call but not the second?

**Answer:** As for repeating the call, it adds emphasis in alerting them and rousing them from the state of heedlessness. It also shows that they are his people and his kin, and that they are in what will destroy them, while he knows the way to their deliverance. Advising them is obligatory for him, so he grieves for them and treats them gently. By this he seeks to make them not suspect him, for their joy is his joy and their grief is his grief, and so that they will accept his counsel to them. This is like Ibrahim (peace be upon him) repeating the call in advising his father: ﴿O my father, O my father﴾.

As for the use of the conjunction *wa*, the second call comes before a statement that explains and elaborates a *mujmal* (a general or summary statement), so it takes the ruling of what precedes it, which is that *wa* cannot be used. The third call, however, comes before a statement that does not have this status. One says *da'ahu ila kadha* and *da'ahu lahu* (he called him to such-and-such, and he called him for it), just as one says *hadahu ila al-tariq* and *hadahu lahu* (he guided him to the road, and he guided him for it). The words ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾ mean "of His lordship." The negation of knowledge here means the negation of the thing known. It is as if he said: "And associate with Him what is not a god, and how can what is not a god be known as a god?"

[[Mahmud said: The meaning of the negation of knowledge is the negation of the thing known, as if he said: "And associate with Him what is not a god, and how can what is not a god be known as a god?" Ahmad said: This is of the kind of the line of poetry:

*On a trackless, faded way, whose landmark one cannot be guided by*

That is, it has no landmark by which one is guided. Al-Zamakhshari's statement here is stronger than his statement on the words of God, related from Pharaoh: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾.]]

La jarama (lā jarama): this is said in accordance with the school of the Basrans: lā is a rejection of what his people called him to. Jarama: a verb meaning "it is right/necessary" (ḥaqqa), and "an" with what follows it is its subject, i.e., it is right and necessary that the invalidity of his call (be established). Or it means "earned" (kasaba), from the words of God Most High, ﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾ (5:2); meaning: that call earned for him the invalidity of his call, in the sense that nothing resulted from it except the manifestation of the invalidity of his call.

It is permissible to say: "an lā jarama" is analogous to "lā budda" (there is no escape), a verb from al-jarm, which is cutting, just as "baddā" is a verb from al-tabdīd, which is dispersing. Just as the meaning of "lā budda annaka tafʿalu kadhā" is "there is no departure from you doing such-and-such," so too "lā jarama anna lahum al-nār" means: there is no cutting off of that; meaning, they perpetually deserve the Fire, with no cessation of their deserving it and no severance, because the invalidity of the idols' call is constant, i.e., it will not cease to be invalid so as to turn into truth. It is transmitted from the Arabs: "lā jarama annahu yafʿalu," with the jīm vowelled with a ḍamma and the rāʾ sukūn, on the pattern of "bud"; faʿl and faʿl are brothers, like rushd and rushd, and ʿudm and ʿudm.

Laysa lahu daʿwatun (﴿has no call﴾): its meaning is that what you call me to has no call to itself at all, i.e., it is the due of the one truly worthy of worship to call his servants to obedience to him, and then he calls his servants to it in order to manifest the call of their Lord and what you call to, and to His worship. He does not call to that himself, nor does he claim lordship; and even if he were a rational animal, he would cry out at your calling. As for His words ﴿in this world nor in the Hereafter﴾, it means that in this world he is inanimate and cannot do anything, including answering calls or otherwise; and in the Hereafter, when God brings him into being as an animal, he will disavow those who called to him and those who worshipped him. It has also been said that the meaning is: he has no answering of a call that benefits in this world or in the Hereafter; or a call that is answered; the call that has no answer and no benefit in it is made like "no call," or the answer is named by the name of the call, as the act recompensed is named by the name of the recompense in their saying: "as you judge, so you will be judged." God Most High said: ﴿To Him is the true call; and those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything﴾ (13:14).

al-Musrifīn: from Qatada: the polytheists. From Mujahid: those who shed blood without right. It has also been said: those whose evil outweighs their good are the musrifūn.

It is read: "fa-satadhkurūn" (so you will remember), meaning: so some of you will remember others. ﴿And I commit my affair to God﴾, because they threatened him.

Then Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted (﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾): the severities of their scheming, and what they intended of inflicting various kinds of punishment on those who opposed them. It was also said: he was delivered along with Moses. ﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾ (﴿and there befell the people of Pharaoh the evil of the punishment﴾): what they had intended of torturing the Muslims. ﴿The Fire﴾ is in apposition (badal) to ﴿the worst of punishment﴾. Or it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), as if a questioner had asked, "What is the worst of punishment?" and it was answered, "It is the Fire." Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿they are exposed to it﴾ (yu'radona 'alayha). In this reading there is an exaltation of the Fire and an emphasis on its torment. Their being exposed to it means their being burned by it. It is said: "The leader exposed the captives to the sword" (i.e., 'arada al-imam al-asra 'ala al-sayf) when he killed them with it. It was also recited as ﴿al-nar﴾ in the accusative (al-nasb), and this supports the last reading. Its estimated sense is: "They enter the Fire, being exposed to it." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas), ﴿morning and evening﴾ (ghuduwwan wa 'ashiyyan): at these two times they are tormented with the Fire, and in the interval between them Allah knows best their condition, whether they are tormented with another kind of punishment or are given respite.

It is also permissible that ﴿morning and evening﴾ is an expression for perpetuity: this lasts as long as the world lasts. Then, when the Hour is established, it will be said to them, ﴿Enter, O people of Pharaoh, the most severe punishment﴾ (ادخلوا آل فرعون أشد العذاب). It was also recited as ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh﴾ (adkhilu Al Fir'awn), meaning: it is said to its guardians (khazanah) of Hell, "Admit them." If you say: His saying ﴿and there befell the people of Pharaoh the evil of the punishment﴾ means that what they had intended of plotting against the Muslims returned upon them, like the Arab saying, "Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it headfirst." Then, if the evil of the punishment is explained as the Fire of Hell, their plotting would not have returned upon them, since they are not punished in Hell by their own plot. I say: It is permissible that a person intends harm to a people by drowning them, and then is burned with fire; this is called ḥayq (a befalling), because he intended evil and there befell him what is called evil. It is not a condition of ḥayq that the one who befalls be exactly that same evil. It is also permissible that Pharaoh intended, when he heard the warning of the Muslims about the Fire, and the statement of the believer, ﴿and that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾, to do what Nimrod did and torture them with fire; so there befell him the like of what he had hidden and intended to do. The Qur'anic verse is cited as evidence for establishing the punishment of the grave (ʿadhab al-qabr).

Mention the time when they will argue with one another (يتحاجون), [the followers being] *taba'an* (تَبَعاً) *tibaʿan* (تباعا), like *khadam* (خدم), the plural of *khadim* (خادم, servant). Or it means "possessors of following" (ذوى تبع), that is, *atbaʿ* (أتباع, followers). Or it is used as a descriptive verbal noun (المصدر, *masdar*).

Also read: "kullun" (kullun, with tanwin), "kullan" would be the reading in question. Let me translate precisely.

And it is read: "Kullun" (إن كلا), for emphasis on the subject of inna, and it is a definite noun (ma'rifa), and the tanwin is a replacement for the genitive noun that was omitted, meaning: "innā kullunā" (indeed we all), or "kullunā fīhā" (all of us in it). If you say: Is it permissible for "kullan" to be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) in which the adverb "fīhā" has acted, [i.e., "fīhā" governing it]?

I say: No, because the adverbial of place does not govern a circumstantial accusative that precedes it, as it governs a time/place adverb when it precedes, as you say: "kullu yawmin laka thawb" (every day you have a garment), and you do not say: "qā'iman fī al-dār Zayd" (standing in the house Zayd). ﴿Indeed Allah will judge between His servants﴾, He decided among them and separated, by making the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire.

To the keepers of Hell, those who are charged with punishing its people. If you ask: why was it not said, "those in the Fire for its keepers"? I answer:

Because mentioning Jahannam (Hell) carries awe and dread. It is also possible that Jahannam is the deepest part of the Fire, from the saying "a jahannam well," meaning a well of deep bottom. And the saying about al-Nabigha, "jahannam," was a name given to him because they claimed he would cast poetry in the voice of the one he was attributed to, so he was deep in his knowledge of poetry. [Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'to its keepers'? He answers that mentioning Jahannam carries awe and dread. It is also possible that Jahannam is the deepest part of the Fire, from the saying 'a jahannam well,' i.e. of deep bottom, and al-Nabigha was called al-Jahannam because of the depth of his penetration into poetry." Ahmad said: the first explanation is more evident, and the emphasis in it comes from two aspects. One: placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, which is what he pointed to. The second: mentioning it, which is one thing with an apparent noun different from the first, more terrifying than it, because Jahannam is more terrifying than "the Fire," since "the Fire" is unqualified and Jahannam is the most intense of it.]

As Abu Nuwas said about Khalaf al-Ahmar:

"Whoever does not count knowledge except what he has known, [the knowledge of Khalaf has perished, since Khalaf perished]
A transmitter who does not pick from written pages—
The deep, abundant well of knowledge..."

[Abu Nuwas composed this lament for Khalaf al-Ahmar ibn Ahmad. "Awda" means "perished." "Man la ya'uddu al-'ilma" is a description of Khalaf: i.e., he counts as knowledge only what he knew with certainty and received by instruction, or what he derived by inference from the rules of earlier scholars. He is a "rawiya," i.e., one who transmits much and does not take from books. He is likened to a flourishing garden by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), and "picking" is an imaginative image (takhyil). "Qulaydham" is a well of abundant water. "Al-'aylam" is a pit with much water. "Al-khuff" is one of deep bottom and great depth; he was compared to it in an eloquent comparison, for the abundance of his knowledge and his grasp of deep and hidden meanings.]

And in it are the most obstinate and most rebellious of the disbelievers. Perhaps the angels charged with punishing those are the most responsive to supplication, due to their greater nearness to God Most High. Therefore the people of the Fire seek them out to ask them for supplication: ﴿Did not your messengers come to you with clear proofs?﴾ This is a binding of the proof and a rebuke, and that they neglected the times of supplication and humble entreaty and abandoned the means by which God answers supplications. They say: ﴿Then supplicate yourselves,﴾ for we do not dare to do that, and we do not intercede except under two conditions: that the one for whom intercession is made is not a wrongdoer, and permission for intercession while observing its time, which is before the decisive judgment between the two groups. Their saying ﴿Then supplicate﴾ is not for hoping for benefit, but to show their hopelessness, for if the honored angel's supplication is not heard, how will the disbeliever's supplication be heard?

"Man la ya'uddu al-'ilma" is a description of Khalaf: i.e., he counts as knowledge only what he knew with certainty and received by instruction, or what he derived by inference from the rules of earlier scholars. He is a "rawiya," i.e., one who transmits much and does not take from books. He is likened to a flourishing garden by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), and "picking" is an imaginative image (takhyil). "Qulaydham" is a well of abundant water. "Al-'aylam" is a pit with much water. "Al-khuff" is one of deep bottom and great depth; he was compared to it in an eloquent comparison, for the abundance of his knowledge and his grasp of deep and hidden meanings.]

And in it are the most obstinate and most rebellious of the disbelievers. Perhaps the angels charged with punishing those are the most responsive to supplication, due to their greater nearness to God Most High. Therefore the people of the Fire seek them out to ask them for supplication: ﴿Did not your messengers come to you with clear proofs?﴾ This is a binding of the proof and a rebuke, and that they neglected the times of supplication and humble entreaty and abandoned the means by which God answers supplications. They say: ﴿Then supplicate yourselves,﴾ for we do not dare to do that, and we do not intercede except under two conditions: that the one for whom intercession is made is not a wrongdoer, and permission for intercession while observing its time, which is before the decisive judgment between the two groups. Their saying ﴿Then supplicate﴾ is not for hoping for benefit, but to show their hopelessness, for if the honored angel's supplication is not heard, how will the disbeliever's supplication be heard?

In the life of this world, and on the day when the witnesses stand. That is, in this world and in the Hereafter. The meaning is that He overpowers them in both abodes, with proof and with victory over their opponents. Even if they are defeated in this world at times, as a trial from God, the final outcome belongs to them. God empowers whoever will avenge them against their enemies, even after a time.

Al-ashhad (the witnesses) is the plural of shahid, as in sahib and as-hab. It means the guardian angels, the prophets, and the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), as in ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [2:143].

The second day is a substitute for the first. It may mean that they will offer an excuse, but it will not benefit them because it is false. It may also mean that they will not offer any excuse, and that even if they did, it would not be accepted. [[Mahmud said: "It may mean that they will offer an excuse, but it will not benefit them, because it is false. It may also mean that they do not offer excuses, and if they did offer one, it would not be accepted." Ahmad said: "These are the two possibilities in God's words ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [40:18]. But between the two passages there is a difference that makes one the reverse of the other. Here, if the meaning is that they have no excuse at all, then He has negated the attribute of an excuse, namely the benefit for which an excuse is sought, in order to cut off their hope that they might offer excuses at all. It is as if it were said: if the fruit of an excuse does not come about, how can something without fruit occur? In the earlier verse, negating the subject was a means of negating the attribute. For this reason, in this verse the negation falls on the act, while in the earlier verse it fell on the entity to which the act is attributed."]] This is in accordance with God's words ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [77:36]. ﴿For them is the curse﴾, that is, distance from God's mercy, ﴿and for them is the evil abode﴾, that is, the evil abode of the Hereafter, which is its punishment.

It is also recited as "taqum" (it stands) and "la tanfa'" (it will not benefit), with the verb in the feminine (ta') and in the masculine (ya').

He means by "guidance" everything He gave him in matters of religion: the miracles, the Torah, and the laws. ﴿And We caused to inherit the Book, after him, to the Children of Israel﴾, that is, the Torah, ﴿a guidance and a reminder﴾, meaning as direction and admonition. Their being in the accusative is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or as a circumstantial accusative (hal). ﴿People of understanding﴾ are those who believe in it and act by what is in it.
