Therefore be patient. Indeed, the promise of God is true. That is: the support of the messengers is under God's guarantee, and God's guarantee is never broken. He cited Moses and what He gave him of the means of guidance and of victory over Pharaoh and his hosts, and the preservation of the traces of his guidance among the Children of Israel. "And God will support you as He supported them, and make you prevail over all religion, and make the dominion of your community reach the eastern and western parts of the earth. So be patient over what your people make you swallow of distresses, for the final outcome is yours, and what My promise of your support and the elevation of your word has preceded is true. Turn to piety, make up for your lapses by seeking forgiveness, and persist in worshipping your Lord and glorifying Him, ﴿in the evening and the morning﴾." It was also said: they are the two prayers of the afternoon (ʿAṣr) and the dawn (Fajr).

In their breasts there is nothing but pride (kibr), that is, arrogance and self-exaltation, which is the desire for precedence and leadership and that no one be above them. That is why they opposed you and rejected Our signs, fearing that you would surpass them and they would fall under your authority, your command and your prohibition, for prophethood brings under it every kingdom and leadership. Or it is the desire that prophethood be theirs rather than yours, out of envy and transgression. This is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [46:11]. Or it is the desire to repel the signs through disputation. ﴿They will not attain it﴾, i.e., they will not attain the object that pride necessitates and requires, and this is what their desire for leadership, prophethood, or the repelling of the signs aims at.

It has been said: the disputants were the Jews, who used to say: "Our companion, the Messiah son of David, will come out," meaning the Dajjal (the Antichrist), "and his dominion will reach the land and the sea, rivers will flow with him, and he is a sign from the signs of God, and the kingdom will return to us." God called their wishing for this "pride," and denied that they would attain what they wished for. ﴿So seek refuge in God﴾, that is, take refuge in Him from the plotting of one who envies you and transgresses against you. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing of what you say and what they say, the All-Seeing of what you do and what they do﴾. So He is your helper against them and your protector from their evil.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 57:**

If you ask: how is His saying ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ connected to what precedes it? I answer: their disputing about the signs of God involved denying the Resurrection, which is the root and the axis of the dispute. So He argued with the creation of the heavens and the earth, because they acknowledged that God created them and that they are a great creation whose greatness cannot be measured. The creation of people, compared with that, is a small and humble thing. Whoever is able to create them despite their greatness is even more able to create a human being despite his lowliness. This is more eloquent than citing the creation of something similar.

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: how is His saying ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ connected to what precedes it? He answered: their disputing about the signs of God involved denying the Resurrection, which is the root and the axis of the dispute. So He argued with the creation of the heavens and the earth, because they acknowledged that God created them, and that they are a great creation. The creation of people, compared with that, is a small and humble thing. Whoever is able to create them despite their greatness is more able to create the weak human being. This is more eloquent than citing the creation of something similar."

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munir) said: The priority in this argument is established on two levels. The first is what he mentioned: that the one who is able to create the great is more able to create the small and insignificant. The second is that their dispute was about the Resurrection, which is the return (i'adah), and there is no doubt that the originating creation (ibtida') is greater and more manifest than the return. So if the originating creation of the great, namely the heavens and the earth, falls under His power, then the originating creation of the insignificant, namely people, falls under it even more, and their return is more included in power than their origination. Thus it is more appropriate that it be within His power than what they acknowledged, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth, on two levels. To this order the indication was made in His saying, in surah al-Rum: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ ... ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾. So He established that the standing of the heaven and the earth is by His command, that is, their creation is among His signs. How much more so, then, is what is lower than their standing by two levels, namely the return of mankind, which is easier for Him than the origination. This is so that the two mentioned levels are realized. So He said: ﴿And He it is who originates the creation, then repeats it, and it is easier for Him﴾. If you reflect on what you have mentioned, attributed to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, you will know that what he mentioned is the essence of the meaning. So renew your attention to it if you do not know this.]] ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, because they do not look and do not reflect, the heedlessness having overcome them and their following of their desires.

The blind man and the seeing man are given as a parable for the one who does good and the one who does evil. It is read "yatadhakkarun" (with the ya', "they take heed") and "tatadhakkarun" (with the ta', "you take heed"); the ta' is the more comprehensive reading.

The Hour is certainly coming; there is no doubt about it. It must come and there is no question of it. "There is no doubt about it" means that it is not something to be doubted, since there must be a recompense. "But most people do not believe": they do not affirm it as true.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 60:

"Call upon Me" (ud'ūnī): worship Me. The word du'ā' (supplication) is used in the sense of ʿibādah (worship) many times in the Qur'an, and the proof for this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾ [Qur'an 40:60]. As for al-istijābah (response), it means ath-ithābah (reward). In the tafsir of Mujahid: "Worship Me, and I will reward you." On al-Hasan, when he was asked about it, he said: "Act and rejoice, for it is truly incumbent upon Allah to respond to those who believe and do righteous deeds and to increase them from His bounty." It is related from al-Thawri that he was told: "Call upon Allah," and he said: "Abandoning sins is itself supplication." And in a hadith: "When My servant busies himself with My obedience instead of supplication, I give him the best of what I give those who ask." [This was related by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from Sufyan from Mansur from Malik ibn al-Harith, who said: "Allah says: When My servant is occupied with His praise instead of asking Me, I give him the best of what I give those who ask." This is a mursal report. In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Saʿid: "Whoever is preoccupied with the recitation of the Qur'an instead of asking Me, I give him the best of what I give those who ask."] And al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Supplication is worship," and he recited this verse. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "supplication" and "response" be their apparent meanings, and that by "My worship" is meant "My supplication," because supplication is a branch of worship and one of its most excellent branches. This is confirmed by the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The best worship is supplication." [Related by al-Hakim in his book on supplication through two chains from him.] And from Kaʿb: "Allah gave this Ummah three qualities which He gave to no prophet except a sent messenger: He used to say to every prophet, 'You are a witness over My creation,' and He said to this Ummah: ﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [Qur'an 2:143]. And He used to say, 'There is no hardship upon you,' and He said to us: ﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship﴾ [Qur'an 5:6]. And He used to say, 'Call upon Me, and I will respond to you,' and He said to us: ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ [Qur'an 40:60]." And from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Worship Me, and I will forgive you." This is an explanation of supplication as worship, and then of worship as monotheism. ﴿Humbled﴾ means ṣāghirīn (abased, humbled).

Musbiran (as a predicate of the subject, the act of seeing) is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), because seeing in reality belongs to the people of the day. If you say: why is the night joined with the object of purpose (li-), and the day with the circumstantial accusative (hal)? Why not make both circumstantial accusatives, or both objects of purpose, so that the correspondence is observed? I say:

They are equivalent in meaning, because each of them performs the function of the other. And if it were said, "that you may see in it" (li-tubsiru fihi), the eloquence contained in the metaphorical attribution would be lost. And if it were said "sakinan" (at rest), while the night may be described as still in reality, do you not see the expression "a still night" (layl saj) and "a calm with no wind in it" (sakin la rih fihi)? The literal would not be distinguished from the metaphorical.

If you say: then why not say "li-mufaddil" (for one who bestows favour) or "li-mutafaddil" (for one who is bounteous)? I say: because the purpose is to render the favour indefinite, and to make it a favour which no other favour can equal, and this is only achieved through the genitive construction (bi-l-idafa).

If you say: then why not say "wa-lakinna aktharahum" (but most of them), so that the mention of "people" is not repeated? I say: in this repetition there is a specification of the ingratitude of the people themselves, and that it is they who deny the favour of God and do not give thanks for it, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful﴾, ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾, ﴿Indeed, mankind is wrongdoing and disbelieving﴾.

That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of everything; there is no god but He. These are successive predicates: that is, He is the one who combines these attributes of divinity (ulūhiyya) and lordship (rubūbiyya), and the creation and origination of everything; nothing is beyond His power. As for unity (waḥdāniyya), He has no second. ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ That is: how, and in what way, are you diverted from worshipping Him to worshipping idols? Then he mentions that everyone who denies the signs of Allah, and does not reflect upon them, and has no resolve to seek the truth and no fear of the consequence: ﴿they are turned away, just as those were turned away.﴾ It is also read "Khāliqu kulli shay'" in the accusative, as a specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). And "tu'fakūn" is read with both the letter tā' and the letter yā'.

This is also another indication of His distinguishing Himself by special acts: that He made the earth a resting place (mustaqarran), and the sky a building (bina'an), meaning a dome (qubba). From this comes the word abniya (dwellings) of the Arabs for their tents (madarib), because the sky, to the eye, appears like a dome pitched over the surface of the earth. "And He shaped you and perfected your forms (fa-ahsana suwarakum)." It is also read with a kasra on the sad (suwarikum), and the meaning is the same. It has been said: He did not create any animal with a more beautiful form than the human being. And it has been said: He did not create them upside down like the beasts, as in His saying, "in the best of stature (fi ahsani taqwim)." "So call upon Him, making your worship sincerely (mukhlisina) for Him in religion (al-din)," meaning obedience free from shirk and showing-off (riya'), "saying: 'Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"

And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: whoever says "There is no god but Allah," let him say immediately after it: "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds."[[Narrated by al-Tabari, and also al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and Ibn Mardawayh, from the narration of al-A'mash from Mujahid from him.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verse 66:

If it is said: Did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) not forbid the worship of idols by means of rational proofs ('aql) before clear proofs came to him from his Lord? I say: Yes. But since the clear proofs (al-bayyinat) strengthen the rational proofs, confirm them, and include their mention, such as His saying, ﴿Do you worship what you carve? And God created you and what you make﴾, and similar alerts to rational proofs, the mention of the clear proofs is a mention of both rational and transmitted (sam') proofs together. He mentioned what indicates both matters together, because the mention of the mutual support of rational proofs and transmitted proofs is stronger in refuting their doctrine, even though rational proofs alone would be sufficient. [[Mahmud said: "If it is said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, had already been made clear about the rational proofs for monotheism before revelation (wahy) came, so on what is the verse to be understood? He answered that the matter is so, but the clear proofs strengthen the rational proofs, confirm them, and include their mention, such as His saying, ﴿Do you worship what you carve? And God created you and what you make﴾, and similar alerts to the rational and transmitted proofs together. He mentioned what indicates both matters together because the mention of both is stronger in refuting their doctrine, even though rational proofs alone would be sufficient."

Ahmad said: The proper course according to the principles of the Sunna (the doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunna, the Sunni school) is to say: As for knowledge of God Most High, knowledge of His oneness, and the impossibility of the idols being gods, this is derived from rational proofs, and rational proofs may appear within the contents of transmitted matters. As for the obligation to worship God Most High and the prohibition of worshipping idols, this is a legal ruling (hukm shar'i) that is derived only from transmitted revelation. Accordingly, the answer to this question is to be set aside. His saying, ﴿I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides God﴾, is intended, and God knows best, to mean the prohibition of worshipping other than God, and this is derived only from God's prohibition of that, not from reason. But al-Zamakhshari's principle requires that the prohibition of worshipping other than God Most High be received from reason before the revelation of the Law (shar'), since reason, in his view, judges by the rule of goodness and ugliness (al-tahsin wa-l-taqbih, the ethical categories of good and evil). For this reason he raised the objection and needed to answer it. Then his statement in the answer, that the proofs of the Law strengthen the proofs of reason, is weak, given his belief that reason indicates the ruling with certainty. What is certain, how can it admit increase and confirmation? Certain matters do not vary in their establishment.]].

For the purpose of "li-tablughu ashuddakum" (so that you may reach your full strength): it is connected to a verb that has been omitted, its implied sense being: "then He lets you live so that you may reach..." And likewise "li-takunu" (so that you may become). As for "wa-li-tablughu ajalan musamman" (and so that you may reach an appointed term), its meaning is: "and We do that so that you may reach an appointed term," which is the time of death. It was also said: the Day of Resurrection.

It was read as "shuyukhan" with a kasra on the shin, and as "shaykhan" in the singular, like His saying "tiflan" (as a child). The meaning is: each one of you. Or he limited it to the singular because the purpose is to explain the category. "Min qablu" (before this): before old age, or before these states, when one comes out as a miscarried fetus. "Wa-la'allakum ta'qilun" (so that you may reason): about what is in that of lessons and proofs.

So when He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is—without effort or toil. He made this a consequence of His power over giving life and causing death, and of the rest of what was mentioned of His acts, which indicate that no object of power can elude Him. It is as if he said: from that power is this: when He decrees a matter, it is the easiest and swiftest of things.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 40, verses 69–76:**

"With the Book": with the Qur'an. "And with that which We sent with Our messengers": with the scriptures.

If you say: Is His saying ﴿But soon they will know, when the shackles are around their necks﴾ equivalent to your saying "I will fast tomorrow" when you mean yesterday?

I say: The meaning is "when" (idh), but since the future matters in God's reports are certain and definite, He expressed them with the wording of the past tense, "was" and "found," while the meaning is the future.

It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he read ﴿and the chains, they will be dragged﴾ with the accusative (al-salasila) and with a fatha on the yāʾ (yusḥabūna), as a coordination of a verbal sentence on a nominal one. And from him: ﴿and the chains, they will be dragged﴾ with the meaning "with the chains."

Its explanation: If it had been said "their necks are in the shackles" in place of ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾, it would have been correct and sound. Since the two are alternating expressions (ʿibāratān muʿtaqibatān), the phrase ﴿and the chains﴾ was construed in line with the other expression. A parallel to this is:

*Ill-omened men who do not reform their clan,*
*nor is there a crow-caller except with the parting of its crow.*

As if it had been said: "with reformers." It was also read: ﴿and with the chains, they will be dragged into the Fire, and then they will be kindled﴾ (yusjarūna), from *sajara al-tannūr*, meaning he filled the oven with fuel. From this comes *al-sajīr* ("the intimate friend"), as if he were filled with love; that is, full. Its meaning: they are in the Fire, and it encompasses them, and they are kindled with the Fire, their insides filled with it. From this is His saying: ﴿the Fire of God, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾. "O God, protect us from Your Fire, for we seek refuge in Your neighborhood."

﴿They have strayed from us﴾: they have vanished from our eyes, so we do not see them and do not benefit from them.

If you say: Did you not mention, in explaining His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾, that they are paired with their gods? How can they be with them if they have strayed from them?

I say: It is possible that they stray from them when they are rebuked and told: "Where are those you associated besides God, so that they may come to your aid and intercede for you?"; and that they are with them at other times (*sāʾir al-awqāt*, meaning the rest of the times after the time of rebuke); and that they are with them at all their times. However, since those gods did not benefit them, it is as if they had strayed from them.

﴿Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before﴾: that is, it has become clear to us that they were nothing, and that we were not worshipping anything by worshipping them, as you say: "I thought that so-and-so was something, but when you tested him you found no good in him."

﴿Thus God leads astray the disbelievers﴾: like the straying of their gods from them; He leads them astray from their gods, so that even if they seek the gods, or the gods seek them, they will not meet.

﴿That is because of your exulting in the earth without right, and because of your insolence﴾: that straying is due to what you had of exultation and insolence without right, which is association and worship of idols.

Al-Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf* on surah 40, verses 79–81:

*Al-an'am* (the livestock): camels specifically. If you ask why He said ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنْهَا وَلِتَبْلُغُوا عَلَيْهَا﴾ ("that you may ride some of them and reach your needs upon them") and did not say "that you may eat from them and attain benefits," or why He did not say "some of them you ride and some of them you eat, and upon them you are carried," then the answer is as follows. Mahmud said: "If you ask, 'Why was it not said: that you may ride some of them, that you may eat from them, and that you may reach [your needs], and some of them you ride and some of them you eat, and upon them you are carried?' He answered that riding includes riding in military campaigns and on pilgrimage, and reaching a need includes emigrating from one land to another to establish religion or to seek knowledge. These are religious purposes, either obligatory or recommended, and they are what the wisdom of the Wise intends. As for eating and attaining benefits, they belong to the category of the permissible (mubah), which the Will does not pertain to."

Ahmad said: This is an answer that is bound to collapse, founded upon a flimsy principle, namely that the command reverts to the Will. Thus the obligatory and the recommended are willed, because they fall under the command, while the permissible is not willed, because it is not commanded. This is one of the vain notions of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) in denying the inner speech (kalam al-nafs), so we shall not prolong our breath on it. The principle of the People of Truth (ahl al-haqq) is that there is no connection between command and will: He may command what He does not will, and will what He does not command. Therefore the correct answer is that the important aim of the livestock and its well-known benefit is in fact riding and carrying one's needs upon them through journeys and travel in pursuit of one's aims. For this reason He mentioned these two here linked with the lam that indicates causation and purpose. As for eating and the rest of the benefits, such as wool, hair, and milk, and what is similar to them, although they are obtained from them, they are not specific to them in the way riding and carrying and their consequences are. Rather, eating is most common with sheep, especially the ewes; for this reason sacrificial animals are chosen from them. Hence these benefits were stripped of any indication of purpose by merely stating their existence in them, not linked with anything that shows they are the intended aim.

﴿وَعَلَيْهَا حَاجَةٌ فِي صُدُورِكُمْ﴾ ("and upon them is a need in your breasts")? I say: in riding is riding in pilgrimage and military campaigns, and in reaching a need is emigrating from one land to another to establish religion or to seek knowledge. These are religious purposes, either obligatory or recommended, which the will of the Wise pertains to. As for eating and attaining benefits, they belong to the category of the permissible, which His will does not pertain to.

Note on the phrase "the permissible which the will does not pertain to": this is based on the Mu'tazila position that will means command, so it pertains only to what is required. According to Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), will is an attribute that specifies the possible with some of what is permissible for it, so it pertains to all possible things, as established in the science of tawhid (theology). (ʿ)

As for the meaning of His words ﴿وَعَلَيْهَا وَعَلَى الْفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ﴾ ("and upon them and upon the ships you are carried"): it does not mean that you are carried upon the livestock alone, but rather upon them and upon the ships, on land and at sea. If you ask, "Why was it not said: 'and in the ships,' as He said ﴿قُلْنَا احْمِلْ فِيهَا مِنْ كُلٍّ زَوْجَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ ('We said: Carry in it two of every kind')?"

I say: the meaning of *al-iy'a'* (placing into a container) and the meaning of *al-isti'la'* (being upon something) are both correct, because the ship is a container for those who are in it, a carrier for them, which they are upon. Since both meanings are valid, both expressions are valid. Furthermore, the phrase ﴿وَعَلَيْهَا﴾ is made to correspond and pair with ﴿أَيَّ آيَاتِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("which of the signs of Allah"), which came in the widespread dialect. As for your saying "then which of the signs of Allah," it is rare, because distinguishing between masculine and feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, as in *himar* and *himara* ("donkey" and "she-donkey"), is unusual, and it is even more unusual with *ayy*, because of its indefiniteness.

and the traces (āthāran) in their palaces and their fortifications. It is also said: their walking on foot, because of the greatness of their bodies. "Mā" in fa-mā aghnā ʿanhum is either negative or implicitly interrogative, and its place is in the accusative; the second (mā) is relative or verbal-infinitival, and its place is in the nominative. "They rejoiced in the knowledge they had" (fa-firaḥū bimā ʿindahum mina l-ʿilm): there are several interpretations concerning it.

First: he meant the knowledge that came in the manner of mockery, in His words, Exalted is He, "Nay, their knowledge has failed concerning the Hereafter" (bal ādārak ʿilmuhum fī l-ākhirah): i.e., their knowledge in the Hereafter, that they used to say, "We will not be raised, nor punished," and "I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I shall surely find there something better than this as a resting-place" (wa-mā aẓunnu s-sāʿata qāʾimatan wa-la-in rujiʿtu ilā rabbī inna lī ʿindahu lalḥusnā), and "I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I shall surely find there better than these as a resting-place" (wa-mā aẓunnu s-sāʿata qāʾimatan wa-la-in ruddittu ilā rabbī la-ajidanna khayran minhā munqalaban). They used to rejoice in this and repel by it the clear signs and the knowledge of the prophets, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Every party rejoicing in what they have" (kullu ḥizbin bimā ladayhim firaḥūn).

Second: he means the knowledge of the philosophers and materialists among the people of Yunan (Greece), and when they heard of God's revelation they rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge. It is related from Socrates that he heard of Moses, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and it was said to him: "If you were to emigrate to him," and he said: "We are a refined people, so we have no need of one who would refine us."

Third: the phrase "they rejoiced in what they had of knowledge" is put, while they had no knowledge at all, in place of "they rejoiced in what came to them of knowledge," as an exaggeration in negating their joy in revelation, which calls for the utmost joy and gladness, together with mockery of the extent of their ignorance and their emptiness of knowledge.

Fourth: it is meant that they rejoiced at what the messengers had of knowledge, a joy of laughing at it and ridiculing it; as if He said: they mocked the clear signs and what they brought of the knowledge of revelation, exulting and gloating. The proof of this is His words: "And there encompassed them what they used to mock" (wa-ḥāqa bihim mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn).

Fifth: the joy is attributed to the messengers. Its meaning: when the messengers saw their persistent ignorance and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end and the punishment that would befall them for their ignorance and mockery, they rejoiced in the knowledge they had been given and thanked God for it, and there befell the disbelievers the recompense of their ignorance and mockery.

It is permissible that by what they rejoiced in of knowledge he means: their knowledge of worldly affairs and their understanding of its management, as He, Exalted, said: "They know an outward aspect of the life of this world, while concerning the Hereafter they are heedless" (yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran mina l-ḥayāti d-dunyā wa-hum ʿani l-ākhirati hum ghāfilūn), "That is the extent of their knowledge" (dhālika mablaghuhum mina l-ʿilm). So when the messengers came to them with the sciences of religion—which is the farthest thing from their knowledge, since it prompts renunciation of the world and restraint (al-ẓalf) from pleasures and desires [[the word "al-ẓalf" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ẓalifat nafsī ʿan kadhā—with kasra—yaẓlaf ẓalfan, i.e., I restrained. (ʿ)]]—they paid them no heed, belittled them and mocked them, and believed that there was no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of benefits than their own, so they rejoiced in it.

First: he meant the knowledge that came in the manner of mockery, in His words, Exalted is He, "Nay, their knowledge has failed concerning the Hereafter" (bal ādārak ʿilmuhum fī l-ākhirah): i.e., their knowledge in the Hereafter, that they used to say, "We will not be raised, nor punished," and "I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I shall surely find there something better than this as a resting-place" (wa-mā aẓunnu s-sāʿata qāʾimatan wa-la-in rujiʿtu ilā rabbī inna lī ʿindahu lalḥusnā), and "I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I shall surely find there better than these as a resting-place" (wa-mā aẓunnu s-sāʿata qāʾimatan wa-la-in ruddittu ilā rabbī la-ajidanna khayran minhā munqalaban). They used to rejoice in this and repel by it the clear signs and the knowledge of the prophets, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Every party rejoicing in what they have" (kullu ḥizbin bimā ladayhim firaḥūn).

Second: he means the knowledge of the philosophers and materialists among the people of Yunan (Greece), and when they heard of God's revelation they rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets in comparison with their own knowledge. It is related from Socrates that he heard of Moses, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and it was said to him: "If you were to emigrate to him," and he said: "We are a refined people, so we have no need of one who would refine us."

Third: the phrase "they rejoiced in what they had of knowledge" is put, while they had no knowledge at all, in place of "they rejoiced in what came to them of knowledge," as an exaggeration in negating their joy in revelation, which calls for the utmost joy and gladness, together with mockery of the extent of their ignorance and their emptiness of knowledge.

Fourth: it is meant that they rejoiced at what the messengers had of knowledge, a joy of laughing at it and ridiculing it; as if He said: they mocked the clear signs and what they brought of the knowledge of revelation, exulting and gloating. The proof of this is His words: "And there encompassed them what they used to mock" (wa-ḥāqa bihim mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn).

Fifth: the joy is attributed to the messengers. Its meaning: when the messengers saw their persistent ignorance and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end and the punishment that would befall them for their ignorance and mockery, they rejoiced in the knowledge they had been given and thanked God for it, and there befell the disbelievers the recompense of their ignorance and mockery.

It is permissible that by what they rejoiced in of knowledge he means: their knowledge of worldly affairs and their understanding of its management, as He, Exalted, said: "They know an outward aspect of the life of this world, while concerning the Hereafter they are heedless" (yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran mina l-ḥayāti d-dunyā wa-hum ʿani l-ākhirati hum ghāfilūn), "That is the extent of their knowledge" (dhālika mablaghuhum mina l-ʿilm). So when the messengers came to them with the sciences of religion—which is the farthest thing from their knowledge, since it prompts renunciation of the world and restraint (al-ẓalf) from pleasures and desires [[the word "al-ẓalf" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ẓalifat nafsī ʿan kadhā—with kasra—yaẓlaf ẓalfan, i.e., I restrained. (ʿ)]]—they paid them no heed, belittled them and mocked them, and believed that there was no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of benefits than their own, so they rejoiced in it.

The Arabic sources in this passage are rendered as follows:

Al-ba's: the severity of the punishment. From it is the words of God Most High ﴿with a painful punishment﴾.

If you ask: what is the difference between God Most High's words ﴿then their faith did not benefit them﴾ and what would be said if it were stated, "then their faith did not benefit them"? I answer: it is of the kind found in His words ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾, and the meaning is: it was not valid and not fitting that their faith should benefit them.

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: what is the difference between His words, 'then their faith did not benefit them,' and what would be said if it were, 'then it did not benefit them?' He answered that the meaning of kana ('was') here is its meaning in His words ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾, meaning: it was not fitting and not valid that their faith should benefit them. Ahmad said: The kana whose usage was made flexible by treating its nun like weak letters (huruf al-'illah), so that it is dropped for the jussive, is the kana that is most commonly used and whose occurrences recur most in speech. As for this kana, it is not so flexible that it may be extended by deletion; rather, it is like sana and hana in rarity. Therefore it is better to keep it in its familiar function. The benefit of its occurrence in this verse and similar ones is to emphasise the negation of the verb it governs, by counting both aspects of its negation: generally, in terms of existence, and specifically, in terms of this verse for example, so that it is as if it were negated twice. And God knows best."]]

If you ask: how did these fa' particles follow one another in succession? I answer: as for His words ﴿so what they had gained did not avail them﴾, it is the result of His words ﴿they were more numerous than them﴾. As for His words ﴿when their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, it functions as an explanation and elaboration of His words ﴿so what they had gained did not avail them﴾, like your saying: "Zayd was given wealth, so he withheld what was good and did not do good to the poor." His words ﴿when they saw Our punishment﴾ follow His words ﴿when their messengers came to them﴾, as if He had said: "they disbelieved, then when they saw Our punishment they believed." Likewise:

﴿then their faith did not benefit them﴾ follows "their faith" when they saw God's punishment. ﴿The way of God﴾ holds the position of ﴿the promise of God﴾ and similar emphatic verbal nouns. ﴿Then﴾ (hunalika) is a place used metaphorically for a time, meaning: they lost at the time of seeing the punishment. Likewise His words ﴿and there the falsifiers lost﴾ after His words ﴿but when the command of God comes, it is judged with truth﴾, meaning: they lost at the time the command of God came, or at the time of judgment with truth.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the chapter of the Believer, no spirit of a prophet, nor of a truthful one, nor of a martyr, nor of a believer will remain but that it prays for him and asks forgiveness for him."

[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may God be pleased with him).]
